title: Marbury v. Madison (1803)
summary: A ministerial duty imposed by law on an executive officer can be enforced by the courts, but the Supreme Court cannot issue the writ in an original action because Congress cannot expand the original jurisdiction Article III fixes.
notes:
Key line: But where a specific duty is assigned by law, and individual rights depend upon the performance of that duty, it seems equally clear that the individual who considers himself injured, has a right to resort to the laws of his country for a remedy. (Chief Justice Marshall)

Citation: 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137 (1803).

Cornell LII Wex on this case (https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/marbury_v_madison_(1803)): Marbury v. Madison (1803) was the U.S. Supreme Court case that established the Supreme Court’s power of judicial review. (Read the opinion here). After President John Adams lost the 1800 election, but before he left office, he appointed Marbury as a justice of the peace and signed the commission. Soon thereafter, Thomas Jefferson became President of the United States and refused to allow Secretary of State James Madison to deliver the commission to Marbury. Marbury sued Madison in the Supreme Court to get his commission via a writ of mandamus. Under Justice John Marshall, the Court specifically held that the provision in the 1789 Act granting the Supreme Court the power to issue a writ of mandamus was unconstitutional. More importantly, however, Marshall’s opinion established that the Supreme Court has the authority, under the Supremacy Clause and Article III, § 2 of the Constitution, to review legislative or executive acts and find them unconstitutional, i.e., the power of judicial review. The Court also delineated the limits of the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction, namely, stating that political questions are not reviewable by the federal courts. It also described the limitations on federal courts’ jurisdiction set forth in Article III of the Constitution. While Marbury v. Madison limited federal court’s jurisdiction, it cemented the Court’s status as the ultimate interpreter of the Constitution.  lawsuits-court

sections.Parties: The applicants were William Marbury, Dennis Ramsay, Robert Townsend Hooe and William Harper, whom President John Adams had nominated as justices of the peace for the District of Columbia in the final days of his term and whom the Senate had confirmed. The respondent was James Madison, Secretary of State under President Jefferson, who withheld their signed and sealed commissions. Charles Lee, who had been Attorney General under Adams, moved for the applicants. Madison made no appearance. Witnesses included Jacob Wagner and Daniel Brent, clerks of the State Department, and Attorney General Levi Lincoln, who answered questions in writing.
sections.Material Facts: Under the Act of February 27, 1801 concerning the District of Columbia, President Adams nominated the applicants as justices of the peace for five-year terms, the Senate advised and consented, and Adams signed the commissions on March 3, 1801, his last full day in office. The Secretary of State affixed the seal of the United States. The commissions were never delivered; when Jefferson took office Madison withheld them. The applicants' requests to Madison for the commissions and to the Senate for a certificate of confirmation were refused. At the December 1801 term they moved in the Supreme Court for a rule ordering Madison to show cause why a mandamus should not issue commanding delivery. Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 authorized the Court to issue writs of mandamus to persons holding office under the authority of the United States. Testimony from the clerks established that the commissions had been signed and sealed and were in the Department.
sections.Procedural History: The applicants brought an original action in the Supreme Court in December 1801 for a rule to show cause, supported by affidavits. The rule issued and was served, but Madison did not respond. At the February 1803 term the Court heard the applicants' evidence and Charles Lee's argument; no one appeared for the Secretary. On February 24, 1803, Chief Justice Marshall delivered the opinion of the Court, joined by the other participating Justices. The Court held that the applicants had a vested right to their commissions and that mandamus was the proper remedy against a ministerial officer, but that section 13 of the Judiciary Act, read to confer original mandamus jurisdiction, exceeded Article III and was void. The rule was discharged and the writ denied.
sections.Issue: Chief Justice Marshall stated three questions. First, does the applicant have a right to the commission he demands, which depends on whether the appointment was complete before delivery? Second, if he has the right and it has been violated, do the laws of his country afford him a remedy, which required deciding whether the Secretary of State's withholding of the commission was a political act beyond judicial examination or the neglect of a ministerial duty that courts can compel? Third, if a remedy exists, is it a mandamus issuing from the Supreme Court, which required construing section 13 of the Judiciary Act and Article III of the Constitution.
sections.Holding: Marbury had a right to the commission. The appointment was complete when the President signed the commission and the Secretary sealed it; delivery is not necessary, and a justice of the peace appointed for five years is not removable at will, so the right vested. The laws afford a remedy. Where the head of a department acts as the President's political agent his acts are examinable only politically, but where a specific duty is assigned by law and individual rights depend on its performance, the injured person may resort to the courts; recording and delivering the commission was such a ministerial duty, and mandamus is the proper form. But the Supreme Court cannot issue it. Article III gives the Court original jurisdiction only in cases affecting ambassadors and those in which a State is a party, Congress cannot add to it, and a law repugnant to the Constitution is void. Rule discharged.
sections.Reasoning: Marshall reasoned that the President's power of nomination and appointment ends with his signature on the commission; the Secretary's sealing is a ministerial act that records an appointment already made, and the commission is evidence of the appointment, not its substance. Because Congress gave the office a fixed term, the appointee gained a legal right that the Executive could not revoke. A government of laws would forfeit that title if the law gave no remedy for a vested legal right. Marshall then drew the line that this course studies: the Secretary of State acts in two capacities. As the President's confidential agent in political matters he answers only to the President and the political process. But Congress had also charged him by statute with public duties, and in performing duties enjoined by law he is a ministerial officer, uncontrollable by the President and compellable by mandamus like any other person holding office under the United States. Withholding Marbury's commission was such a case. Turning to jurisdiction, Marshall read section 13 as authorizing the Court to issue mandamus in an original proceeding, then held that Article III's distribution of original and appellate jurisdiction would be meaningless surplusage if Congress could rearrange it. A written constitution is paramount law; an act repugnant to it is void; and courts, which must decide what the law is when statute and constitution conflict, are bound by the constitution rather than the statute.

topics.lrs-o-ministerial-duties: The assigned dicta classify delivery of the completed commission as a compulsory act affecting individual rights and thus appropriate for judicial compulsion.
topics.lrs-n-discrete-required-action: Marbury's ministerial-duty/mandamus distinction underlies § 706(1)'s limit to discrete, legally required agency action.

learning.separateOpinions: None. Chief Justice Marshall delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court of the Justices who participated.
